sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Construction inspection plays an integral role in producing a high-quality soil nail wall. Inspection covers five aspects: material conformance, construction method conformance, identification of changed site conditions, short-term load testing, and long-term monitoring. The inspector must understand design drawings and specifications and maintain daily installation logs. Short-term monitoring is typically performed during construction; long-term monitoring is conducted by the Owner.
sections.body:
Inspection activities, when appropriately conducted, play an integral role in the production of a high-quality soil nail wall. This chapter focuses on the most common aspects of soil nail wall inspection and monitoring. The discussion is applicable regardless of the contracting approach followed and what party is assigned inspection duties. Inspection involves evaluation of: (i) conformance of system components to material specifications; (ii) conformance of construction methods to execution specifications; (iii) identification of site or soil conditions that require adjustment to installation procedures or to the original design; (iv) conformance to short-term performance specifications (i.e., load testing); and (v) long-term monitoring, if required by contract.

Monitoring activities assess the performance of the soil nail wall and may include short-term and long-term measurements. Short-term monitoring is usually limited to measurements during and shortly after construction and may include lateral wall deflection, ground movement, and nail load testing. Long-term monitoring is less typical and usually includes a continuation of short-term measurements. Short-term monitoring may be performed by the Owner or the Contractor; long-term monitoring is usually conducted by the Owner.

The inspector must understand all relevant aspects of soil nail wall construction and must be intimately familiar with the design drawings and specifications. The inspector is responsible for maintaining soil nail installation logs, a daily log and field book, and for recording all relevant aspects of construction activities.
key_points: Five inspection aspects: material conformance, method conformance, changed conditions, load testing, long-term monitoring
Applicable to all contracting approaches and inspection parties
Inspector must be familiar with design drawings, specifications, and all construction aspects
Inspector maintains installation logs, daily log, and field book
Short-term monitoring by Owner or Contractor; long-term monitoring by Owner
Reference: Soil Nailing Field Inspector's Manual (Porterfield et al. 1994)
sections.applicability: General framework for inspection and monitoring responsibilities during soil nail wall construction and post-construction performance assessment.

sections.title: Inspection of Construction Materials
sections.summary: Materials quality is controlled by visual examination, manufacturer certifications, and laboratory testing. Steel components (tendons, bearing plates, WWM) are accepted by mill certifications; cement is accepted by certification and unconfined compressive testing on grout. All materials must be stored to prevent deterioration. Corrosion protection systems on tendons must be inspected upon delivery and before use; damaged encapsulated sheaths must be repaired or the tendon replaced.
sections.body:
The quality of all materials is controlled by one or a combination of: (i) visual examination for defects due to poor workmanship, contamination, or damage from handling; (ii) certification by the manufacturer or supplier that materials comply with design and specification requirements; and (iii) laboratory testing of representative samples. Steel components (tendons, bearing plates, nuts, washers, WWM, reinforcing bars) are normally accepted based on mill certifications. Cement is accepted based on certification pending results of unconfined compressive testing on grout. Centralizers, coatings, grout additives, sheathing, geocomposite drainage material, and piping are normally accepted based on manufacturer certificates. Water used in grout or shotcrete must be free from chemical or organic material that may negatively affect its performance; potable water is generally suitable without testing.

All materials must be kept in a suitable location and protected to prevent deterioration. Cement must be kept dry and elevated from the ground. Tendons must be placed on supports to prevent direct contact with the ground and with appropriate spacing to prevent excessive bending. Other steel components and drainage materials should be stored in suitable containers.

The corrosion protection systems of all tendons must be inspected at the project site, prior to acceptance and use. Tendons with damaged corrosion protection must be repaired, if possible, or replaced. Encapsulated tendons are usually delivered to the site assembled; inspection must include visual examination of the corrugated sheath, couplers, and end caps for tears, holes, or compromised seals. Epoxy-coated bars must be inspected for coating damage; damaged areas require touch-up repair with approved epoxy patching compound. Galvanized bars require inspection for coating damage and holiday testing in critical service environments.
key_points: Materials acceptance: mill certifications (steel), manufacturer certifications (admixtures/coatings), lab testing (cement/grout)
Potable water acceptable for grout or shotcrete without testing
Cement: must be kept dry and elevated; avoid over-stacking bags
Tendons: store on supports with adequate spacing to prevent bending
Corrosion protection must be inspected before acceptance; damaged encapsulation requires repair or replacement
Encapsulated tendons: inspect corrugated sheath, couplers, end caps for tears, holes, compromised seals
sections.applicability: Quality acceptance and storage requirements for soil nail wall materials at the project site, with emphasis on corrosion protection inspection.

sections.title: Inspection of Construction Activities: Organization and Excavation
sections.summary: Inspection during construction should be performed by qualified individuals — the geotechnical engineer, wall designer, specialty contractor, or a third party. Two types of excavation are inspected: mass excavation (site grading and equipment access) and bench excavation to the finished wall line. Inspectors must verify the excavation does not encroach on the completed wall, and must check cut face stability and unexpected soil conditions that may require design modification.
sections.body:
Inspection during construction of a soil nail wall should be carried out by qualified individuals. Depending on the project, inspection may be entirely carried out by the Geotechnical Engineer, the wall Designer or Specialty Contractor, a third party, or a combination. A third-party inspection firm may not be qualified to perform certain specialized inspection tasks such as evaluating unexpected soil conditions, drill-hole performance, or load testing interpretation; in those cases, the geotechnical engineer or wall designer must be engaged.

The two types of excavation inspected are: (1) mass excavation, conducted to provide equipment access and general site grading; and (2) bench excavations required for construction of the soil nail wall to the finished wall line (the 'neat line' shown on plans). During mass excavation, the inspector must verify that the excavation does not encroach upon the partially completed soil nail wall. During bench excavation, the inspector must verify that the excavated face is cut to within the specified tolerances of the final wall line.

The inspector must be alert to conditions that differ from those anticipated in the design. Signs of instability (caving, sloughing, water seepage) must be noted and communicated to the design engineer. Zones of soft soil or fill not considered during design may require design revision. The inspector must note and record: (i) cut face conditions (standup time, caving, seepage); (ii) excavation dimension and location relative to plans; (iii) any dewatering requirements; and (iv) any drainage problems that should be addressed by additional drainage features.
key_points: Qualified inspectors required: geotechnical engineer, wall designer, specialty contractor, or third party
Third-party inspectors may not be qualified for specialized tasks — engage design engineer as needed
Mass excavation must not encroach on partially completed wall
Bench excavation to finished wall line (neat line) must be within specified tolerances
Record cut face conditions: standup time, caving, seepage, soft zones
Unexpected soft soil or fill not in design may require design modification
sections.applicability: Qualification requirements for inspection personnel and inspection procedures for mass and bench excavations during soil nail wall construction.

sections.title: Drilling Inspection
sections.summary: Drill holes must be located and oriented within the tolerances specified on plans. Hole angle is measured using an angle tool on the drill mast; care must be taken that the mast angle reflects the actual tendon inclination at the cut face. The inspector must record drill-hole length, diameter, orientation, soil conditions encountered, drilling obstructions, groundwater, and any cave-ins. The drilling log is the primary construction record for each nail.
sections.body:
The drill holes should be located and oriented as shown on the plans and within the tolerances in the specifications. Any deviation in location or orientation beyond the specified tolerances must be noted and communicated to the Owner. The angle of the drill mast is typically measured using an angle tool placed directly on the mast; care must be taken that the mast angle is representative of the tendon inclination as it enters the excavation face.

Drilling inspection requirements include recording the following for each drill hole: (i) planned and actual drill-hole location (distance along wall face from reference point, elevation); (ii) planned and actual inclination angle; (iii) drill-hole length; (iv) drill-hole diameter; (v) soil conditions encountered, noting changes in soil type or consistency; (vi) caving or sloughing; (vii) presence of groundwater or artesian conditions; (viii) obstructions encountered; and (ix) return flush behavior.

The inspector should note whether return flush becomes clogged, there is hydraulic connection with other drill holes or the ground surface, or if heaving results from drilling fluid pressurization. Subsurface conditions revealed during drilling that differ significantly from those anticipated in design must be reported to the geotechnical engineer promptly. Conditions such as unexpected voids, organic layers, or groundwater may require adjustment to the nail installation procedures, nail spacing, or the overall wall design.
key_points: Drill-hole location and orientation must be within specified tolerances; deviations reported to Owner
Hole angle measured with angle tool on drill mast; must represent actual tendon inclination at face
Record for each hole: location, inclination, depth, diameter, soil conditions, caving, groundwater, obstructions
Observe return flush: clogging, hydraulic connection with other holes, heaving from fluid pressure
Significant deviations from expected conditions must be reported to the geotechnical engineer promptly
Unexpected voids, organics, or groundwater may require design modification
sections.applicability: Inspection procedures for drill-hole installation in soil nail walls, including recording requirements and response to unexpected subsurface conditions.

sections.title: Tendon Installation and Grouting
sections.summary: Tendons must be verified to meet length, diameter, grade, centralizer spacing, and corrosion protection requirements before installation. Inability to insert a tendon to full length indicates unacceptable caving. Grouting integrity cannot be directly verified, but is assessed indirectly through pre-grout hole inspection and volume of grout injected. Grout volume should be 100 to 130 percent of the theoretical hole volume; outside this range requires notification and remedial action. Specific gravity (target 1.8 to 1.9) is the primary QC indicator.
sections.body:
The inspection personnel must verify that each tendon meets the length, diameter, steel grade, centralizer, and corrosion protection requirements in the plans and specifications. The tendon must be inserted into the hole to the minimum specified length; inability to do so indicates unacceptable conditions caused by caving or sloughing of the hole. Tendon insertion problems must be immediately reported to the Owner.

Grouting inspection focuses on: (i) verifying grout is injected by tremie pipe inserted to the bottom of the drill hole in a continuous process; (ii) controlling tremie pipe withdrawal rate to ensure the pipe end is always below the grout surface; (iii) recording the volume of grout placed. When hollow-stem auger drilling methods are used, the Contractor should not be allowed to reverse auger rotation during extraction, as this forces soil to mix with the grout and reduces grout-ground bond strength.

The volume of injected grout must be at least equal to the theoretical volume of the hole; typically 10 to 30 percent larger is expected. If the volume of grout injected is less than 100 percent or greater than 130 percent of theoretical, the Contractor and Owner must be notified and remedial measures undertaken if needed.

For production soil nails, specific gravity of the freshly prepared grout should be the primary QC mechanism, preferred over compression testing. In neat cement grout, specific gravity correlates directly with water-cement ratio and hence strength. The target specific gravity is typically 1.8 to 1.9. Grout cubes are prepared at the start of the project to correlate specific gravity with compressive strength (ASTM C109); thereafter, specific gravity monitoring at each batch serves as the daily QC tool. Grout cube testing frequency and specimen molding requirements must be specified. For HBSNs, drilling grout may have a specific gravity of 1.4 to 1.6; a heavier final grout (1.8 to 1.9) is pumped after bar installation, and the nail is complete when the heavier grout returns to the excavation face.
key_points: Verify each tendon: length, diameter, grade, centralizer spacing, corrosion protection before insertion
Inability to insert tendon to full length indicates caving — report immediately
Grout by tremie to bottom of hole; withdraw tremie keeping end below grout surface
Target grout volume: 100-130% of theoretical hole volume; outside range requires notification
Specific gravity target 1.8-1.9 for neat cement grout — primary QC indicator, preferred over cube testing
HBSN: drilling grout SG 1.4-1.6; final grout SG 1.8-1.9; nail complete when heavy grout returns at face
Hollow-stem auger: do not reverse auger during extraction — mixes soil into grout
sections.applicability: Inspection procedures for soil nail tendon installation and grouting, including QC requirements for grout volume and specific gravity.

sections.title: Geocomposite Strip Drains and Wall Facing
sections.summary: Geocomposite strip drains must be placed vertically at specified intervals after nail installation, continuous from top to bottom of wall, with proper orientation of the permeable side toward the cut face. Shotcrete facing requires an experienced nozzleman; critical inspection points include reinforcing steel placement, cold joint preparation, nozzle distance (2-5 ft wet-mix, 3-6 ft dry-mix), and minimum shotcrete thickness. Bearing plates must be positioned while shotcrete is wet, without voids underneath.
sections.body:
Once the final wall line excavation and nail installation are complete for each lift, geocomposite strip drains are placed vertically at specified intervals. Strip drains must be continuous from top to bottom of the wall. The inspector should verify that strip drains are installed in accordance with the construction drawings. Often, strip drains are fitted with an impermeable protective liner on one side; the impermeable side must face the shotcrete facing, and the permeable side must face the cut. Drains must be properly connected at the base to the footing drain and weepholes in the facing.

After geocomposite strip drains are installed, the reinforcing steel is placed and shotcrete applied to the lines and grades specified. The WWM and reinforcing steel must be installed with proper dimensions, at the specified locations, and with the prescribed overlap length. The most critical factor in ensuring good-quality shotcrete facing is a nozzleman with experience in applying shotcrete. Specifications may require certification by ACI or the American Shotcrete Association (ASA) and a pre-qualification test panel prior to production work.

Recommended shotcrete application practices include: (i) hold nozzle perpendicular to the exposed surface, except when shooting around reinforcing bars; (ii) optimum nozzle distance 2 to 5 ft for wet-mix, 3 to 6 ft for dry-mix; (iii) start placement at the bottom; (iv) do not allow voids to form behind bars, plates, or mesh; (v) use screen boards, guide wires, and depth spacers to establish sharp edges and accurate lines. The inspector must verify that the shotcrete attains the minimum specified thickness within tolerance, and that bearing plates with headed studs are positioned while the shotcrete is wet and without voids underneath. For cast-in-place final facing, standard reinforced concrete inspection procedures apply.
key_points: Strip drains: placed vertically at specified spacing, continuous top to bottom, impermeable liner toward facing
Connect strip drains at base to footing drain and wall face weepholes
Nozzleman must be experienced; ACI or ASA certification may be required; pre-qualification test panel
Wet-mix shotcrete nozzle distance: 2-5 ft; dry-mix: 3-6 ft; start placement at bottom
Do not allow voids behind bars, mesh, or plates
Bearing plates must be installed while shotcrete is wet, without voids underneath
Cold joint must be cleaned before placing overlying shotcrete lift
sections.applicability: Inspection requirements for geocomposite strip drain installation and shotcrete wall facing construction in soil nail walls.

sections.title: Load Testing: Overview and Test Types
sections.summary: Three types of load tests verify soil nail performance: Verification tests on sacrificial pre-production nails confirm pullout capacity and bond strengths used in design; Proof tests on 5 percent of production nails confirm uniform performance throughout the wall; Creep tests (part of verification and proof testing) measure nail movement at constant load over 10 to 60 minutes to ensure tolerable creep. A standard practice is to complete testing in each row prior to progressing to the next lower level.
sections.body:
Soil nails are load tested in the field to verify that the nail design loads can be carried without excessive movements and with an adequate factor of safety. Testing also verifies the adequacy of the Contractor's drilling, installation, and grouting operations. If ground conditions or installation procedures change, additional testing may be required. Standard practice is to complete testing in each row of nails prior to progressing to the next lower level of excavation.

Verification Load Tests: Conducted on non-production, sacrificial nails prior to construction (and sometimes during production where conditions change) to verify compliance of pullout capacity with values used in design. Verification tests should be conducted to a maximum load that induces bond stresses at least equal to the nominal bond resistance used in design. When intended to reach complete pullout, an oversized tendon may be needed to ensure the ground-grout bond fails before the steel. Verification tests are not conducted on production nails.

Proof Tests: Conducted during construction on a minimum of 5 percent of total production nails. Intended to verify that there are no significant variations in nail performance throughout the wall. Nails selected for proof testing should reflect records of installation issues (irregular drilling progress, lower-than-typical grout take, or nails that had to be re-installed). Proof tests are single-cycle tests loaded to a maximum proof test load (PTL).

Creep Tests: Performed as part of verification and proof testing. Consist of measuring soil nail movement at a constant load over a specified period of time (10 to 60 minutes). Performed to ensure that the nail can safely carry the intended load throughout the service life with low or predictable creep displacements.
key_points: Three load test types: verification (pre-production, sacrificial), proof (5% of production nails), creep
Verification tests: confirm pullout capacity and bond strength used in design; may be taken to failure
Proof tests: single-cycle, minimum 5% of production nails; use installation records to select candidates
Creep tests: part of verification and proof tests; measure movement at constant load over 10-60 min
Complete testing in each row before progressing to next lower excavation level
Additional testing required if ground conditions or installation methods change
sections.applicability: Overview of soil nail load testing types and triggers for additional testing during soil nail wall construction.

sections.title: Load Test Equipment and Verification Testing Procedures
sections.summary: Testing uses a center-hole hydraulic jack and pump with a jacking frame or reaction block sized to avoid overstressing the facing. A bondbreaker sleeve creates an unbonded length that must extend at least 1 ft beyond the failure surface. Verification test load (VTL) = rPO × LB_VT; bond length is limited by nail tensile capacity (Eqs 9.1-9.2 for Grade 60/75 and Grade 150). Loading follows Table 9.1: increments from 0.13 to 1.00 VTL with the 0.75 VTL step held for 60 minutes for creep. Acceptance requires no pullout below VTL and total movement exceeding 80% of the theoretical elastic elongation.
sections.body:
A center-hole hydraulic jack and hydraulic pump apply the test load to a nail tendon. The axis of the jack and the axis of the nail must be aligned to ensure uniform loading. A jacking frame or reaction block is installed between the shotcrete or excavation face and the jack; the reaction block must be sized appropriately to avoid overstressing the shotcrete. The jacking frame should not react directly against the nail grout column during testing. An alignment load (AL, typically <= 0.025 VTL) is applied before readings are zeroed.

Verification test nails must have a defined bonded length (LB_VT) and a temporary unbonded length created by a bondbreaker sleeve. The unbonded length must extend from behind the bearing plate to the top of the grouted length, and must be at least 1 ft beyond the potential failure surface. Maximum bond length to prevent tensile failure before ground failure (Grades 60 and 75): LB_VT_max = CRTY × At × fy / rPO; for Grade 150 and high-strength steel: LB_VT_max = CRTU × At × fu / rPO, where CRTY = 0.9, CRTU = 0.8, At = area of test tendon, rPO = pi × qu × DDH.

Verification Test Load: VTL = rPO × LB_VT (Equation 9.3). Theoretical elastic elongation of the unbonded length: delta_VTL = VTL × L_unbonded / (E × At) (Equation 9.4, E = 29,000 ksi).

Load schedule (Table 9.1): AL (1 min), 0.13 VTL (10 min), 0.25 VTL (10 min), 0.38 VTL (10 min), 0.50 VTL (10 min), 0.63 VTL (10 min), 0.75 VTL Creep Test (60 min, recorded at 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 10, 20, 30, 50, 60 min), 0.88 VTL (10 min), 1.00 VTL (10 min). Movements must be recorded after each increment and at each time step.

Acceptance criteria: (i) pullout does not occur at loads less than 1.00 VTL; (ii) total nail movement at VTL exceeds 80 percent of the theoretical elastic elongation delta_VTL; (iii) creep movement meets criteria in Section 9.4.5.
key_points: Center-hole hydraulic jack + reaction block; jack axis must align with nail axis; reaction block not against grout column
Verification nails: temporary unbonded length with bondbreaker sleeve extending >= 1 ft past failure surface
Eq 9.1: LB_VT_max = 0.9*At*fy/rPO (Grade 60/75); Eq 9.2: LB_VT_max = 0.8*At*fu/rPO (Grade 150)
Eq 9.3: VTL = rPO * LB_VT; Eq 9.4: delta_VTL = VTL * L_unbonded / (E * At), E = 29,000 ksi
Acceptance: no pullout < 1.00 VTL; measured movement > 80% of delta_VTL; creep < criteria

sections.title: Proof Tests, Creep Tests, and Strain Gauges
sections.summary: Proof tests are single-cycle tests on production nails using a 10-ft bond length (minimum) and a 3-ft minimum unbonded length inside the drill hole. PTL = rPO × LB_PT (Eq 9.7). Load schedule (Table 9.2): 0.17, 0.33, 0.50, 0.67, 0.83, 1.00 PTL (creep at 1.00 PTL). Acceptance: no pullout < 1.00 PTL, movement > 80% elastic elongation. Creep acceptance: < 0.04 in between 1 and 10 min at 0.75 VTL (or 1.00 PTL); < 0.08 in between 6 and 60 min. Strain gauges measure axial load distribution along the nail tendon.
sections.body:
Proof tests are single-cycle tests in which the load is applied in increments to a maximum proof test load (PTL). Proof test nails must have a bonded length and a temporary unbonded length with a bondbreaker sleeve. The unbonded length must extend from the back of the bearing plate to the top of the grouted length and must be at least 3 ft within the drill hole. Maximum bond lengths: for Grades 60 and 75: LB_PT_max = CRTY × At × fy / rPO (Equation 9.5); for Grade 150: LB_PT_max = CRTU × At × fu / rPO (Equation 9.6); selected bond length is min(LB_PT_max, 10 ft).

Proof Test Load: PTL = rPO × LB_PT (Equation 9.7). Theoretical elastic elongation: delta_PTL = PTL × L_unbonded / (E × At) (Equation 9.8). Load schedule (Table 9.2): AL, 0.17 PTL, 0.33 PTL, 0.50 PTL, 0.67 PTL, 0.83 PTL, 1.0 PTL (Creep Test). Each increment held for at least 10 minutes. Acceptance criteria: (i) no pullout at loads less than 1.0 PTL; (ii) total movement at PTL > 80 percent of delta_PTL; (iii) creep movement meets criteria in Section 9.4.5.

Creep tests are conducted at a specified constant test load, with displacements recorded at specified time intervals. Results are plotted as deflection versus log-time. Acceptance criteria require that: (i) creep movement between the 1- and 10-minute readings at 0.75 VTL (verification tests) or 1.0 PTL (proof tests) is less than 0.04 in.; (ii) creep movement between the 6- and 60-minute readings at 0.75 VTL is less than 0.08 in. If the 1-to-10-minute criterion is exceeded in a proof test, PTL must be maintained for an additional 50 minutes and the 10-to-60-minute criterion re-evaluated.

Strain gauges can be used to measure axial strain of the tendon during testing. Using E = 29,000 ksi, axial load may be calculated at each gauge location. Multiple spot-weldable strain gauges along the tendon permit determination of the variation of axial loads along the nail length, and the average mobilized bond resistance between consecutive gauges under any applied load. This distribution is used to evaluate whether the bond stress distribution is reasonable and consistent with design assumptions.
key_points: Proof tests on production nails: min 5 ft unbonded length (3 ft inside drill hole), min 10 ft bond length preferred

sections.title: Instrumentation and Performance Monitoring
sections.summary: Performance monitoring is recommended for critical or unusual soil nail walls (road widening under bridges, high surcharge, first-time Owner installation). Monitored parameters include horizontal wall face movement (inclinometers 3-8 ft behind facing), vertical and horizontal top-of-wall movement (optical survey), ground cracking and settlement, and groundwater levels. A monitoring and action plan must specify trigger levels for increased monitoring and construction stoppage. Instruments include inclinometers, survey prisms, strain gauges, and nail head load cells.
sections.body:
Performance monitoring should be included in any critical or unusual soil nail wall installation. Examples include: walls constructed for road widening projects under existing bridges; walls with high surcharge loading; and permanent walls constructed by an Owner for the first time. Monitoring instrumentation for such walls should include inclinometers, top-of-wall survey points, load cells, and strain gauges.

The most significant indicator of overall performance is the amount of deformation of the wall or slope during and after construction. A performance-monitoring plan should typically include measurement of: (i) horizontal movements of the wall face using surface markers with optical surveying and inclinometer casings installed 3 to 8 ft behind the facing (not farther than 30 percent of wall height for a single row); (ii) vertical and horizontal movements of the top of wall facing and ground surface behind the facing; (iii) ground cracking location and width; (iv) surface settlement behind the wall; and (v) groundwater levels near the wall.

The monitoring and action plan should specify: (i) monitoring frequency (typically daily during active construction, then decreasing after completion); (ii) trigger levels at which monitoring frequency increases; (iii) threshold values at which construction stops and the engineer is notified; and (iv) contingency measures. Trigger and threshold values are project-specific and typically expressed as maximum allowable horizontal and vertical displacements related to the wall height and local conditions.

Instruments include: (i) Inclinometers — most comprehensive data on wall deformation; in-place inclinometers allow rapid measurement throughout full depth without physical probe insertion but must be verified periodically with manual readings. (ii) Survey Points — reflector prisms read by optical surveying or EDM to 0.1 in. accuracy within 300 ft; automated total stations reduce reading error. (iii) Strain Gauges — vibrating wire type is most common in the U.S.; attached to nail tendon using sister bars; measure axial load distribution as excavation progresses. (iv) Load Cells at Nail Head — Wheatstone-resistance bridge type; measure loads at the facing over time; results must be interpreted carefully as load cells can occasionally provide inaccurate readings.
key_points: Monitoring required for critical walls: under existing bridges, high surcharge, first Owner installation
Inclinometers placed 3-8 ft behind facing, not farther than 30% of wall height for single-row monitoring
Action plan must specify: monitoring frequency, trigger levels (increased monitoring), and threshold values (stop construction)
Survey prisms readable to 0.1 in. within 300 ft; automated total stations reduce reading errors
Strain gauges: vibrating wire type, attached via sister bars, measure axial load distribution along nail
Nail head load cells measure facing loads over time; interpret carefully — occasional inaccurate readings
Monitoring frequency: daily during active construction, then decreasing after completion
sections.applicability: Performance monitoring plan requirements and instrument types for critical and unusual soil nail wall installations.
